Analysis of Muon’s Convergence and Critical Batch Size

Naoki Sato naoki310303@gmail.com Affiliation: Meiji University    Hiroki Naganuma naganuma.hiroki@mila.quebec Affiliation: Université de Montréal, Mila    Hideaki Iiduka iiduka@cs.meiji.ac.jp Affiliation: Meiji University
Abstract

This paper presents a theoretical analysis of Muon, a new optimizer that leverages the inherent matrix structure of neural network parameters. We provide convergence proofs for four practical variants of Muon: with and without Nesterov momentum, and with and without weight decay. We then show that adding weight decay leads to strictly tighter bounds on both the parameter and gradient norms, and we clarify the relationship between the weight decay coefficient and the learning rate. Finally, we derive Muon’s critical batch size minimizing the stochastic first-order oracle (SFO) complexity, which is the stochastic computational cost, and validate our theoretical findings with experiments.

††firstpage: 1

1 Introduction

Optimization algorithms are fundamental to the training of deep neural networks (DNNs). Since the introduction of stochastic gradient descent (SGD) [1], numerous improved methods have been proposed. Among these, adaptive gradient-based algorithms such as Adam [2] and its variant AdamW [3] have become the standard choice in modern deep learning. Recently, Muon [4] was proposed as a new, theoretically-grounded optimizer for the linear layers of neural networks. While SGD vectorizes weight matrices, Muon preserves their matrix structure and uses gradient orthogonalization to compute the search direction. The simplest form of the search direction Ot∈ℝm×nO_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n} in Muon is obtained by orthogonalizing the gradient momentum matrix Mt∈ℝm×nM_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}, i.e.,

Ot:=argminO:ℝm×n:‖O‖2≤1∥O−Mt∥F.\displaystyle O_{t}:=\underset{O:\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}:\|O\|_{2}\leq 1}{\operatorname{argmin}}\|O-M_{t}\|_{F}.

If the singular value decomposition (SVD) of MtM_{t} is given by Ut​St​Vt⊤U_{t}S_{t}V_{t}^{\top}, then Ot=Ut​Vt⊤O_{t}=U_{t}V_{t}^{\top}, where Ut∈ℝm×r,St∈ℝr×r,Vt∈ℝn×rU_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times r},S_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times r},V_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times r}, and r>0r>0 is the rank of MtM_{t}. In general, SVD calculations are computationally expensive; the core idea of Muon is to leverage the Newton–Schulz iteration [5, 6, 7, 8] to perform this orthogonalization efficiently [9].

Several studies have reported the strong empirical performance of Muon [4, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14]. In particular, [10] demonstrates that Muon is effective for training large-scale LLMs and suggests it has the potential to replace AdamW as the standard optimizer. However, the theoretical understanding of Muon’s convergence remains limited, and a formal justification for its strong performance over AdamW is lacking. This work aims to bridge this gap by providing a rigorous convergence analysis of Muon. Furthermore, since the batch size is a critical hyperparameter for managing computational costs in large-scale training, we also derive the optimal batch size for Muon.

Our main contributions are as follows:

  • •

    We provide a convergence analysis for four variants of Muon: with and without Nesterov momentum, and with and without weight decay (Theorems 3.1-3.4). The resulting upper bounds on the average expected gradient norm, 1T​∑t∈[T]𝔼⁡[‖∇f​(Wt)‖F]\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t\in[T]}\mathbb{E}\left[\|\nabla f(W_{t})\|_{F}\right], for each variant are summarized in Table 1.

  • •

    We prove that including weight decay yields tighter theoretical bounds on both the parameter and gradient norms (Propositions 3.1 and 3.2), and we provide experimental results to support this finding. We also clarify the relationship between the learning rate and the weight decay coefficient required for the convergence of Muon with weight decay.

  • •

    We derive the critical batch size for the four Muon variants and show that the variant with Nesterov momentum and weight decay achieves the largest critical batch size.

2 Preliminaries

2.1 Notations and Definition

Let ℕ\mathbb{N} be the set of non-negative integers. For m∈ℕ∖{0}m\in\mathbb{N}\setminus\{0\}, define [m]:={1,2,…,m}[m]:=\{1,2,\ldots,m\}. Let ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} be a dd-dimensional Euclidean space with inner product ⟨⋅,⋅⟩\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle, which induces the norm ∥⋅∥\|\cdot\|. We use lowercase letters for scalars (e.g., OPENa∈ℝ)a\in\mathbb{R}), bold lowercase letters for vectors (e.g., 𝒂∈ℝd\bm{a}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}), and uppercase letters for matrices (e.g., A∈ℝm×nA\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}). 𝒂⊤∈ℝ1×d\bm{a}^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{1\times d} and A⊤∈ℝn×mA^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times m} denote the transposes of 𝒂∈ℝd\bm{a}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} and A∈ℝm×nA\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}, respectively. For a square matrix A=(ai​j)∈ℝn×nA=(a_{ij})\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}, the trace is defined as tr⁡(A):=∑i=1nai​i\operatorname{tr}(A):=\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_{ii}. For all vector 𝒙,𝒚∈ℝd\bm{x},\bm{y}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, the Euclidean inner product defined as ⟨𝒙,𝒚⟩2:=𝒙⊤​𝒚\langle\bm{x},\bm{y}\rangle_{2}:=\bm{x}^{\top}\bm{y} and the Euclidean norm defined as ‖𝒙‖2:=⟨𝒙,𝒙⟩2\|\bm{x}\|_{2}:=\sqrt{\langle\bm{x},\bm{x}\rangle}_{2}. For all matrices A,B∈ℝm×nA,B\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}, the Frobenius inner product defined as ⟨A,B⟩F:=tr⁡(A⊤​B)\langle A,B\rangle_{F}:=\operatorname{tr}(A^{\top}B) and the Frobenius norm defined as ‖A‖F:=⟨A,B⟩F\|A\|_{F}:=\sqrt{\langle A,B\rangle_{F}}. The model is parameterized by a matrix W∈ℝm×nW\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}, which is optimized by minimizing the empirical loss function f⁡(W):=1N​∑i∈[N]fi​(W)f(W):=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i\in[N]}f_{i}(W), where N∈ℝN\in\mathbb{R} is the number of training data and fi​(W)f_{i}(W) is the loss function for W∈ℝm×nW\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n} and the ii-th training data 𝒛i\bm{z}_{i} (i∈[N])(i\in[N]). 2.3 Assumptions

We make the following standard assumptions:

Assumption 2.1.

f:ℝm×n→ℝf\colon\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\to\mathbb{R} is continuously differentiable and LL-smooth, i.e., for all X,Y∈ℝm×nX,Y\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n},

(i) For each iteration tt,

𝔼ξt,i​[𝖦ξt,i​(Wt)]=∇f​(Wt).\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\xi_{t,i}}\left[\mathsf{G}_{\xi_{t,i}}(W_{t})\right]=\nabla f(W_{t}).

𝔼ξt,i​[‖𝖦ξt,i​(Wt)−∇f​(Wt)‖F2]≤σ2.\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\xi_{t,i}}\left[\|\mathsf{G}_{\xi_{t,i}}(W_{t})-\nabla f(W_{t})\|_{F}^{2}\right]\leq\sigma^{2}.

For each iteration tt, Muon samples a mini-batch 𝒮t⊂𝒮\mathcal{S}_{t}\subset\mathcal{S} and estimates the full gradient ∇f\nabla f as

∇f𝒮t(Wt):=1b∑i∈[b]𝖦ξt,i(Wt)=1b∑{i:𝒛i∈𝒮t}∇fi(Wt).\displaystyle\nabla f_{\mathcal{S}_{t}}(W_{t}):=\frac{1}{b}\sum_{i\in[b]}\mathsf{G}_{\xi_{t,i}}(W_{t})=\frac{1}{b}\sum_{\{i\colon\bm{z}_{i}\in\mathcal{S}_{t}\}}\nabla f_{i}(W_{t}).

3 Analysis of Muon’s convergence

3.1 Muon without weight decay

The following is a convergence analysis of Muon (Algorithm 1) without weight decay (the proofs of Theorems 3.1 and 3.2 are in Appendices B.1 and B.2, respectively).

Theorem 3.1 (Muon w/o Nesterov and w/o Weight Decay).

Suppose that Assumptions 2.1-2.3 hold and the sequence (Wt)t∈ℕ(W_{t})_{t\in\mathbb{N}} generated by Muon (Algorithm 1). Then, for all t∈ℕt\in\mathbb{N},

1T​∑t=0T−1𝔼⁡[‖∇f​(Wt)‖F]≤𝒪⁡(1T+1−βb+n).\displaystyle\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\mathbb{E}\left[\|\nabla f(W_{t})\|_{F}\right]\leq\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{1}{T}+\frac{1-\beta}{b}+n\right).
Theorem 3.2 (Muon w/ Nesterov and w/o Weight Decay).

Suppose that Assumptions 2.1-2.3 hold and the sequence (Wt)t∈ℕ(W_{t})_{t\in\mathbb{N}} generated by Muon (Algorithm 1). Then, for all t∈ℕt\in\mathbb{N},

1T​∑t=0T−1𝔼⁡[‖∇f​(Wt)‖F]≤𝒪⁡(1T+(2​β+1)​(1−β)2⋅1b+n).\displaystyle\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\mathbb{E}\left[\|\nabla f(W_{t})\|_{F}\right]\leq\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{1}{T}+\frac{(2\beta+1)(1-\beta)}{2}\cdot\frac{1}{b}+n\right).

Theorems 3.1 and 3.2 show that Muon with and without Nesterov momentum have similar upper bounds on their convergence. However, the constant term in the bound, which is independent of the number of iterations TT and batch size bb, is slightly smaller when Nesterov momentum is used (see Appendices B.1 and B.2). These theorems also establish that Muon reduces the norm of the full gradient at a rate of approximately 1/T1/T, regardless of whether Nesterov momentum is used.

3.2 Muon with weight decay

The following proposition establishes a key result for the Muon (Algorithm 1) with weight decay (the proofs of Propositions 3.1 and 3.2 are in Appendices C.1 and C.2, respectively).

Proposition 3.1 (Boundedness of Sequences in Muon with Weight Decay).

Suppose that Assumptions 2.1-2.3 hold and the sequence (Wt)t∈ℕ(W_{t})_{t\in\mathbb{N}} generated by Muon (Algorithm 1) with η≤1λ\eta\leq\frac{1}{\lambda}. Then, for all t∈ℕt\in\mathbb{N},

‖Wt‖F≤{(1−η​λ)t​‖W0‖F+nλ if ​η<1λ,nλ if ​η=1λ.\displaystyle\|W_{t}\|_{F}\leq\begin{cases}(1-\eta\lambda)^{t}\|W_{0}\|_{F}+\frac{\sqrt{n}}{\lambda}&\text{ if }\ \eta<\frac{1}{\lambda},\\ \frac{\sqrt{n}}{\lambda}&\text{ if }\ \eta=\frac{1}{\lambda}.\end{cases}
Proposition 3.2 (Boundedness of Gradients in Muon with Weight Decay).

Suppose that Assumptions 2.1-2.3 hold and the sequence (Wt)t∈ℕ(W_{t})_{t\in\mathbb{N}} generated by Muon (Algorithm 1) with η≤1λ\eta\leq\frac{1}{\lambda}. Then, for all t∈ℕt\in\mathbb{N},

‖∇f​(Wt)‖F≤{L​(1−η​λ)t​‖W0‖F+Lλ+L​‖W⋆‖F if ​η<1λ,Lλ+L​‖W⋆‖F if ​η=1λ.\displaystyle\|\nabla f(W_{t})\|_{F}\leq\begin{cases}L(1-\eta\lambda)^{t}\|W_{0}\|_{F}+\frac{L}{\lambda}+L\|W^{\star}\|_{F}&\text{ if }\ \eta<\frac{1}{\lambda},\\ \frac{L}{\lambda}+L\|W^{\star}\|_{F}&\text{ if }\ \eta=\frac{1}{\lambda}.\end{cases}

Proposition 3.1 shows that when η≤1λ\eta\leq\frac{1}{\lambda}, weight decay ensures the parameter norm is almost surely bounded. Furthermore, this upper bound decreases monotonically in tt, converging to nλ\frac{\sqrt{n}}{\lambda} as t→∞t\to\infty as t→∞t\to\infty. The bound is minimized for all tt when η=1λ\eta=\frac{1}{\lambda}. Proposition 3.2 extends this finding to the full gradient norm, which is also almost surely bounded. This bound also decreases monotonically, converging to Lλ+L​‖W⋆‖F\frac{L}{\lambda}+L\|W^{\star}\|_{F} as t→∞t\to\infty. From this result, Corollary 3.1 establishes that Muon converges almost surely. In both cases, the upper bounds are minimized when η=1λ\eta=\frac{1}{\lambda}.

Corollary 3.1.

Suppose that Assumptions 2.1-2.3 hold and the sequence (Wt)t∈ℕ(W_{t})_{t\in\mathbb{N}} generated by Muon (Algorithm 1) with η≤1λ\eta\leq\frac{1}{\lambda}. Then, for all T∈ℕT\in\mathbb{N},

1T​∑t=0T‖∇f​(Wt)‖F≤{L​‖W0‖Fη​λ​T+Lλ+L​‖W⋆‖F if ​η<1λ,Lλ+L​‖W⋆‖F if ​η=1λ.\displaystyle\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=0}^{T}\|\nabla f(W_{t})\|_{F}\leq\begin{cases}\frac{L\|W_{0}\|_{F}}{\eta\lambda T}+\frac{L}{\lambda}+L\|W^{\star}\|_{F}&\text{ if }\ \eta<\frac{1}{\lambda},\\ \frac{L}{\lambda}+L\|W^{\star}\|_{F}&\text{ if }\ \eta=\frac{1}{\lambda}.\end{cases}

While these results suggest that a larger weight decay λ\lambda yields a tighter bound, the condition η≤1λ\eta\leq\frac{1}{\lambda} necessitates a smaller learning rate η\eta. These desirable properties stem from the fact that Muon’s search direction is inherently bounded. A key advantage of this feature is that our analysis does not require the common, and often restrictive, assumption of bounded gradients.

The following is a convergence analysis of Muon (Algorithm 1) with weight decay (the proofs of Theorems 3.3 and 3.4 are in Appendices C.3 and C.4, respectively).

Theorem 3.3 (Muon w/o Nesterov, w/ weight decay).

Suppose that Assumptions 2.1-2.3 hold and the sequence (Wt)t∈ℕ(W_{t})_{t\in\mathbb{N}} generated by Muon (Algorithm 1) with η≤1λ\eta\leq\frac{1}{\lambda}. Then, for all t∈ℕt\in\mathbb{N},

1T​∑t=0T−1𝔼⁡[‖∇f​(Wt)‖F]≤𝒪⁡(1T+(1−β+λ2)​1b+n).\displaystyle\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\mathbb{E}\left[\|\nabla f(W_{t})\|_{F}\right]\leq\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{1}{T}+\left(1-\beta+\frac{\lambda}{2}\right)\frac{1}{b}+n\right).
Theorem 3.4 (Muon w/ Nesterov, w/ weight decay).

Suppose that Assumptions 2.1-2.3 hold and the sequence (Wt)t∈ℕ(W_{t})_{t\in\mathbb{N}} generated by Muon (Algorithm 1) with η≤1λ\eta\leq\frac{1}{\lambda}. Then, for all t∈ℕt\in\mathbb{N},

1T​∑t=0T−1𝔼⁡[‖∇f​(Wt)‖F]≤𝒪⁡(1T+(2​β+1)​(1−β)+λ2⋅1b+n).\displaystyle\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\mathbb{E}\left[\|\nabla f(W_{t})\|_{F}\right]\leq\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{1}{T}+\frac{(2\beta+1)(1-\beta)+\lambda}{2}\cdot\frac{1}{b}+n\right).

Similar conclusions are drawn from Theorems 3.3 and 3.4, which again show a small advantage for using Nesterov momentum (see Appendices C.3 and C.4).

4 Analysis of Muon’s critical batch size

We next introduce the concept of the critical batch size, which is the optimal batch size in terms of computational complexity. We measure this complexity using the stochastic first-order oracle (SFO), which is the total number of stochastic gradient computations. For an optimizer that takes TT steps with a batch size of bb, the SFO complexity is T​bTb. Empirically, for batch sizes up to a certain threshold b⋆b^{\star} (the critical batch size), the number of training steps TT required to train a DNN scales inversely with bb [15, 16, 17]. Beyond b⋆b^{\star}, increasing the batch size yields diminishing returns in reducing TT. The critical batch size b⋆b^{\star} is therefore the batch size that minimizes the SFO complexity T​bTb. Prior work has suggested that the critical batch size depends on the optimizer [18] and has established a theoretical framework for estimating its lower bound [19, 20]. We adopt this framework to analyze the critical batch size of Muon.

Let TMuonT_{\text{Muon}} be the number of steps required for Muon to reach a precision ϵ>0\epsilon>0, such that

1TMuon​∑t=0TMuon−1𝔼⁡[‖∇f​(Wt)‖F]≤ϵ.\displaystyle\frac{1}{T_{\text{Muon}}}\sum_{t=0}^{T_{\text{Muon}}-1}\mathbb{E}\left[\|\nabla f(W_{t})\|_{F}\right]\leq\epsilon.

The critical batch size for Muon, bMuon⋆b_{\text{Muon}}^{\star}, is then defined as bMuon⋆:=argminb∈[n]⁡TMuon​bb_{\text{Muon}}^{\star}:={\operatorname{argmin}}_{b\in[n]}T_{\text{Muon}}b. Based on Theorems 3.1-3.4, we derive the following proposition, which provides bMuon⋆b_{\text{Muon}}^{\star}. The proof is detailed in Appendix D.

Proposition 4.1.

Suppose Assumptions 2.1-2.3 hold. Then, for a given precision ϵ\epsilon, the critical batch size for Muon (Algorithm 1) is as shown in Table 2.

Table 2 indicate that, for a given precision ϵ\epsilon, Muon’s critical batch size is slightly larger when Nesterov momentum and weight decay are used.

5 Numerical Experiments

We conduct a series of experiments to validate our theoretical analysis of Muon. We first examine the convergence conditions and convergence rate, then analyze the critical batch size.

Experimental Setup

We use the CIFAR-10 dataset for our experiments with ResNet-18.

For each experiment, we perform a grid search for hyperparameters, primarily the learning rate, using a base batch size of 512. For other batch sizes, we adjust the learning rate using the square root scaling rule for Muon and AdamW. For Momentum SGD, we test both square root and linear scaling rules. All experiments are run five times with different random seeds, and we report the mean and standard deviation. Further details on the experimental protocol are provided in Appendix E.

Convergence Analysis

First, we empirically validate the stability condition derived in Proposition 3.2. Figure 1 shows the final gradient norm and training loss for ResNet-18 trained with various learning rates (η\eta) at a fixed weight decay (λ\lambda = 0.0625). The vertical dashed line indicates the theoretical stability threshold η=1/λ\eta=1/\lambda = 16.0. As predicted by our theory, the model achieves the lowest gradient norm near this threshold. For learning rates exceeding this value, training becomes unstable, and performance degrades sharply. This trend holds for other weight decay values, as detailed in Appendix F.

Next, we compare the convergence rates of the four Muon variants against AdamW and Momentum SGD. Figure 2 illustrates the training loss and the smoothed gradient norm versus training steps for a batch size of 2048. Consistent with our theoretical bounds in Table 1, Muon with both Nesterov momentum and weight decay converges the fastest among the variants. These results demonstrate that the tighter theoretical bounds translate to faster empirical convergence.

Critical Batch Size

Here, we evaluate training efficiency across various batch sizes by measuring the number of steps and the Stochastic First-order Oracle (SFO) complexity required to reach a target accuracy. The target test and training accuracies were set to 90% and 95%, respectively. As shown in Figure 3, Muon scales more effectively with larger batch sizes compared to baselines. The number of steps to reach the target test accuracy decreases consistently as the batch size increases (left in Figure 3). While Momentum SGD requires more steps within our training schedule, it eventually reaches a comparable accuracy (see Appendix F). The SFO complexity plots (right in Figure 3) highlight Muon’s efficiency, as it achieves the lowest complexity across all tested batch sizes. Notably, we find that including Nesterov momentum shifts the critical batch size (the batch size that minimizes SFO complexity) to the right. This suggests that Nesterov momentum allows for efficient training with even larger batch sizes. Furthermore, Muon’s critical batch size is smaller than that of AdamW, which is a significant practical advantage for reducing computational costs.

6 Related Works

Several studies have investigated the theoretical properties and convergence of Muon. The work of Bernstein and Newhouse connects Muon to applying momentum in the steepest descent direction under a spectral norm constraint [5]. Li and Hong provided a pioneering analysis assuming Frobenius norm Lipschitz smoothness [21]. Pethick et al. studied Muon within the context of optimization methods that use linear minimization oracles (LMOs) on norm balls, providing a convergence rate [22]. Connections to other optimizers have also been established. Shah et al. showed that Shampoo [23] and SOAP [24] reduce to Muon under simplifying assumptions [14]. Kovalev proposed and analyzed a stochastic non-Euclidean trust-region method that includes Muon as a special case [25]. Similarly, An et al. proposed an Adaptive Structured Gradient Optimization (ASGO) algorithm that matches Muon in its momentum-free variant [11]. Other work has explored specific properties and extensions of Muon. Petrov et al. proposed and analyzed a zeroth-order version [26]. Chen et al. demonstrated Muon’s compatibility with the Lion-𝒦\mathcal{K} algorithm [27] and showed that Muon with weight decay implicitly solves an optimization problem with a spectral norm constraint [28]. Shen et al. presented a comprehensive analysis of Muon’s convergence rate in comparison to gradient descent (GD) [29]. The core concepts of gradient orthogonalization and dualization, which are central to Muon, were introduced in the foundational works of [30, 31].

7 Conclusion

This paper establishes a theoretical foundation for Muon, an optimizer that leverages the matrix structure of neural network parameters. We prove convergence for four variants of Muon, including those with and without Nesterov momentum and weight decay. Our analysis demonstrates that incorporating weight decay yields strictly tighter bounds on both parameter and gradient norms, and we clarify the relationship between the weight decay coefficient and the learning rate. Furthermore, we derive a Muon’s critical batch size and experimentally validate our theoretical predictions. Together, these results clarify the advantages of Muon over traditional optimizers and offer practical guidance for its application in large-scale training.

Appendix A Tools for Proof of All Theorems

The results in this section are not new and are presented for reference.

Lemma A.1.

Suppose that Assumptions 2.2(ii) and 2.3 hold for all t∈ℕt\in\mathbb{N}; then,

𝔼𝝃t​[‖∇f𝒮t​(Wt)−∇f​(Wt)‖F2]≤C2b.\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\bm{\xi}_{t}}\left[\|\nabla f_{\mathcal{S}_{t}}(W_{t})-\nabla f(W_{t})\|_{F}^{2}\right]\leq\frac{C^{2}}{b}.
Proof.

Assumptions 2.2(ii) and 2.3 guarantee that

𝔼𝝃t​[‖∇f𝒮t​(Wt)−∇f​(Wt)‖F2]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\bm{\xi}_{t}}\left[\|\nabla f_{\mathcal{S}_{t}}(W_{t})-\nabla f(W_{t})\|_{F}^{2}\right] =𝔼𝝃t​[‖1b​∑i=1b𝖦ξt,i​(Wt)−∇f​(Wt)‖F2]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\bm{\xi}_{t}}\left[\left\|\frac{1}{b}\sum_{i=1}^{b}{\mathsf{G}_{\xi_{t,i}}(W_{t})}-\nabla f(W_{t})\right\|_{F}^{2}\right]
=𝔼𝝃t​[‖1b​∑i=1b𝖦ξt,i​(Wt)−1b​∑i=1b∇f​(Wt)‖F2]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\bm{\xi}_{t}}\left[\left\|\frac{1}{b}\sum_{i=1}^{b}{\mathsf{G}_{\xi_{t,i}}(W_{t})}-\frac{1}{b}\sum_{i=1}^{b}\nabla f(W_{t})\right\|_{F}^{2}\right]
=𝔼𝝃t​[‖1b​∑i=1b(𝖦ξt,i​(Wt)−∇f​(Wt))‖F2]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\bm{\xi}_{t}}\left[\left\|\frac{1}{b}\sum_{i=1}^{b}\left({\mathsf{G}_{\xi_{t,i}}(W_{t})-\nabla f(W_{t})}\right)\right\|_{F}^{2}\right]
=1b2​𝔼𝝃t​[‖∑i=1b(𝖦ξt,i​(Wt)−∇f​(Wt))‖F2]\displaystyle=\frac{1}{b^{2}}\mathbb{E}_{\bm{\xi}_{t}}\left[\left\|\sum_{i=1}^{b}\left({\mathsf{G}_{\xi_{t,i}}(W_{t})-\nabla f(W_{t})}\right)\right\|_{F}^{2}\right]
=1b2​𝔼𝝃t​[∑i=1b‖𝖦ξt,i​(Wt)−∇f​(Wt)‖F2]\displaystyle=\frac{1}{b^{2}}\mathbb{E}_{\bm{\xi}_{t}}\left[\sum_{i=1}^{b}\left\|{\mathsf{G}_{\xi_{t,i}}(W_{t})-\nabla f(W_{t})}\right\|_{F}^{2}\right]
≤σ2b.\displaystyle\leq\frac{\sigma^{2}}{b}.

This completes the proof. ∎

The following lemma is a result established by [32]. In their setting, the algorithm without the momentum term corresponds to the case β1=1\beta_{1}=1, whereas in our setting, it corresponds to β1=0\beta_{1}=0. Therefore, note that the results may appear slightly different.

Lemma A.2.

Suppose that Assumptions 2.1-2.3 hold and the sequence (Wt)t∈ℕ(W_{t})_{t\in\mathbb{N}} generated by Muon (Algorithm 1). Then for all t∈ℕt\in\mathbb{N},

∑t=0T−1𝔼⁡[‖Mt−∇f​(Wt)‖F2]≤21−β​‖M0−∇f​(W0)‖F2+2​(1−β)​σ2b​T+4​L2​η2​n(1−β)2​T,\displaystyle\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\mathbb{E}\left[\|M_{t}-\nabla f(W_{t})\|_{F}^{2}\right]\leq\frac{2}{1-\beta}\|M_{0}-\nabla f(W_{0})\|_{F}^{2}+\frac{2(1-\beta)\sigma^{2}}{b}T+\frac{4L^{2}\eta^{2}n}{(1-\beta)^{2}}T,

and

∑t=0T−1𝔼⁡[‖Mt−∇f​(Wt)‖F]≤22−1+β​‖M0−∇f​(W0)‖F+2​(1−β)​σ2b​T+2​L​η​n1−β​T.\displaystyle\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\mathbb{E}\left[\|M_{t}-\nabla f(W_{t})\|_{F}\right]\leq\frac{\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{2}-\sqrt{1+\beta}}\|M_{0}-\nabla f(W_{0})\|_{F}+\sqrt{\frac{2(1-\beta)\sigma^{2}}{b}}T+\frac{2L\eta\sqrt{n}}{1-\beta}T.
Proof.

From the definition of MtM_{t},

‖Mt−∇f​(Wt)‖F2\displaystyle\|M_{t}-\nabla f(W_{t})\|_{F}^{2}
=∥βMt−1+(1−β)∇f𝒮t(Wt)−∇f(Wt)∥F2\displaystyle\hskip 9.24994pt=\|\beta M_{t-1}+(1-\beta)\nabla f_{\mathcal{S}_{t}}(W_{t})-\nabla f(W_{t})\|_{F}^{2}
=‖β⁡(Mt−1−∇f​(Wt−1))+β⁡(∇f​(Wt−1)−∇f​(Wt))+(1−β)​(∇f𝒮t​(Wt)−∇f​(Wt))‖F2\displaystyle\hskip 9.24994pt=\|\beta(M_{t-1}-\nabla f(W_{t-1}))+\beta(\nabla f(W_{t-1})-\nabla f(W_{t}))+(1-\beta)(\nabla f_{\mathcal{S}_{t}}(W_{t})-\nabla f(W_{t}))\|_{F}^{2}
=β2​‖Mt−1−∇f​(Wt−1)‖F2+β2​‖∇f​(Wt−1)−∇f​(Wt)‖F2+(1−β)2​‖∇f𝒮t​(Wt)−∇f​(Wt)‖F2\displaystyle\hskip 9.24994pt=\beta^{2}\|M_{t-1}-\nabla f(W_{t-1})\|_{F}^{2}+\beta^{2}\|\nabla f(W_{t-1})-\nabla f(W_{t})\|_{F}^{2}+(1-\beta)^{2}\|\nabla f_{\mathcal{S}_{t}}(W_{t})-\nabla f(W_{t})\|_{F}^{2}
+2​β2​⟨Mt−1−∇f​(Wt−1),∇f​(Wt−1)−∇f​(Wt)⟩F\displaystyle\hskip 9.24994pt\hskip 9.24994pt+2\beta^{2}\langle M_{t-1}-\nabla f(W_{t-1}),\nabla f(W_{t-1})-\nabla f(W_{t})\rangle_{F}
+2​β​(1−β)​⟨Mt−1−∇f​(Wt−1),∇f𝒮t​(Wt)−∇f​(Wt)⟩F\displaystyle\hskip 9.24994pt\hskip 9.24994pt+2\beta(1-\beta)\langle M_{t-1}-\nabla f(W_{t-1}),\nabla f_{\mathcal{S}_{t}}(W_{t})-\nabla f(W_{t})\rangle_{F}
+2​β​(1−β)​⟨∇f​(Wt−1)−∇f​(Wt),∇f𝒮t​(Wt)−∇f​(Wt)⟩F\displaystyle\hskip 9.24994pt\hskip 9.24994pt+2\beta(1-\beta)\langle\nabla f(W_{t-1})-\nabla f(W_{t}),\nabla f_{\mathcal{S}_{t}}(W_{t})-\nabla f(W_{t})\rangle_{F}

Therefore, by taking the expectation,

𝔼⁡[‖Mt−∇f​(Wt)‖F2]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\|M_{t}-\nabla f(W_{t})\|_{F}^{2}\right] =β2​𝔼​[‖Mt−1−∇f​(Wt−1)‖F2]+β2​𝔼​[‖∇f​(Wt−1)−∇f​(Wt)‖F2]\displaystyle=\beta^{2}\mathbb{E}\left[\|M_{t-1}-\nabla f(W_{t-1})\|_{F}^{2}\right]+\beta^{2}\mathbb{E}\left[\|\nabla f(W_{t-1})-\nabla f(W_{t})\|_{F}^{2}\right]
+(1−β)2​𝔼​[‖∇f𝒮t​(Wt)−∇f​(Wt)‖F2]\displaystyle\hskip 9.24994pt+(1-\beta)^{2}\mathbb{E}\left[\|\nabla f_{\mathcal{S}_{t}}(W_{t})-\nabla f(W_{t})\|_{F}^{2}\right]
+2​β2​𝔼​[⟨Mt−1−∇f​(Wt−1),∇f​(Wt−1)−∇f​(Wt)⟩F].\displaystyle\hskip 9.24994pt+2\beta^{2}\mathbb{E}\left[\langle M_{t-1}-\nabla f(W_{t-1}),\nabla f(W_{t-1})-\nabla f(W_{t})\rangle_{F}\right].

Here, according to Peter-Paul inequality, for all ϵ>0\epsilon>0, we have

⟨Mt−1−∇f​(Wt−1),∇f​(Wt−1)−∇f​(Wt)⟩F≤ϵ2​‖Mt−1−∇f​(Wt−1)‖F2+12​ϵ​‖∇f​(Wt−1)−∇f​(Wt)‖F2.\displaystyle\langle M_{t-1}-\nabla f(W_{t-1}),\nabla f(W_{t-1})-\nabla f(W_{t})\rangle_{F}\leq\frac{\epsilon}{2}\|M_{t-1}-\nabla f(W_{t-1})\|_{F}^{2}+\frac{1}{2\epsilon}\|\nabla f(W_{t-1})-\nabla f(W_{t})\|_{F}^{2}.

Therefore, we obtain

𝔼⁡[‖Mt−∇f​(Wt)‖F2]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\|M_{t}-\nabla f(W_{t})\|_{F}^{2}\right] =β2​(1+ϵ)​𝔼​[‖Mt−1−∇f​(Wt−1)‖F2]+β2​(1+1ϵ)​𝔼​[‖∇f​(Wt−1)−∇f​(Wt)‖F2]\displaystyle=\beta^{2}(1+\epsilon)\mathbb{E}\left[\|M_{t-1}-\nabla f(W_{t-1})\|_{F}^{2}\right]+\beta^{2}\left(1+\frac{1}{\epsilon}\right)\mathbb{E}\left[\|\nabla f(W_{t-1})-\nabla f(W_{t})\|_{F}^{2}\right]
+(1−β)2​𝔼​[‖∇f𝒮t​(Wt)−∇f​(Wt)‖F2].\displaystyle\hskip 9.24994pt+(1-\beta)^{2}\mathbb{E}\left[\|\nabla f_{\mathcal{S}_{t}}(W_{t})-\nabla f(W_{t})\|_{F}^{2}\right].

In addition, from Assumption 2.1,

‖∇f​(Wt−1)−∇f​(Wt)‖F2≤L2​‖Wt−1−Wt‖F2=L2​η2​‖Ot‖F2=L2​η2​n.\displaystyle\|\nabla f(W_{t-1})-\nabla f(W_{t})\|_{F}^{2}\leq L^{2}\|W_{t-1}-W_{t}\|_{F}^{2}=L^{2}\eta^{2}\|O_{t}\|_{F}^{2}=L^{2}\eta^{2}n.

Hence, from Lemma A.1,

𝔼⁡[‖Mt−∇f​(Wt)‖F2]≤β2​(1+ϵ)​𝔼​[‖Mt−1−∇f​(Wt−1)‖F2]+β2​(1+1ϵ)​L2​η2​n+(1−β)2​σ2b.\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\|M_{t}-\nabla f(W_{t})\|_{F}^{2}\right]\leq\beta^{2}(1+\epsilon)\mathbb{E}\left[\|M_{t-1}-\nabla f(W_{t-1})\|_{F}^{2}\right]+\beta^{2}\left(1+\frac{1}{\epsilon}\right)L^{2}\eta^{2}n+\frac{(1-\beta)^{2}\sigma^{2}}{b}.

Then letting ϵ:=1−β2\epsilon:=\frac{1-\beta}{2}, we have

𝔼⁡[‖Mt−∇f​(Wt)‖F2]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\|M_{t}-\nabla f(W_{t})\|_{F}^{2}\right] ≤β2​(3−β)2​𝔼​[‖Mt−1−∇f​(Wt−1)‖F2]+β2​(3−β)1−β​L2​η2​n+(1−β)2​σ2b\displaystyle\leq\frac{\beta^{2}(3-\beta)}{2}\mathbb{E}\left[\|M_{t-1}-\nabla f(W_{t-1})\|_{F}^{2}\right]+\frac{\beta^{2}(3-\beta)}{1-\beta}L^{2}\eta^{2}n+\frac{(1-\beta)^{2}\sigma^{2}}{b}
≤1+β2​𝔼​[‖Mt−1−∇f​(Wt−1)‖F2]+21−β​L2​η2​n+(1−β)2​σ2b\displaystyle\leq\frac{1+\beta}{2}\mathbb{E}\left[\|M_{t-1}-\nabla f(W_{t-1})\|_{F}^{2}\right]+\frac{2}{1-\beta}L^{2}\eta^{2}n+\frac{(1-\beta)^{2}\sigma^{2}}{b}
≤(1+β2)t​‖M0−∇f​(W0)‖F2+{2​L2​η2​n1−β+(1−β)2​σ2b}​∑k=0t−1(1+β2)k\displaystyle\leq\left(\frac{1+\beta}{2}\right)^{t}\|M_{0}-\nabla f(W_{0})\|_{F}^{2}+\left\{\frac{2L^{2}\eta^{2}n}{1-\beta}+\frac{(1-\beta)^{2}\sigma^{2}}{b}\right\}\sum_{k=0}^{t-1}\left(\frac{1+\beta}{2}\right)^{k}
≤(1+β2)t​‖M0−∇f​(W0)‖F2+{2​L2​η2​n1−β+(1−β)2​σ2b}​21−β\displaystyle\leq\left(\frac{1+\beta}{2}\right)^{t}\|M_{0}-\nabla f(W_{0})\|_{F}^{2}+\left\{\frac{2L^{2}\eta^{2}n}{1-\beta}+\frac{(1-\beta)^{2}\sigma^{2}}{b}\right\}\frac{2}{1-\beta}
=(1+β2)t​‖M0−∇f​(W0)‖F2+4​L2​η2​n(1−β)2+2​(1−β)​σ2b.\displaystyle=\left(\frac{1+\beta}{2}\right)^{t}\|M_{0}-\nabla f(W_{0})\|_{F}^{2}+\frac{4L^{2}\eta^{2}n}{(1-\beta)^{2}}+\frac{2(1-\beta)\sigma^{2}}{b}.

Therefore, summing over tt, we have

∑t=0T−1𝔼⁡[‖Mt−∇f​(Wt)‖F2]≤21−β​‖M0−∇f​(W0)‖F2+2​(1−β)​σ2b​T+4​L2​η2​n(1−β)2​T.\displaystyle\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\mathbb{E}\left[\|M_{t}-\nabla f(W_{t})\|_{F}^{2}\right]\leq\frac{2}{1-\beta}\|M_{0}-\nabla f(W_{0})\|_{F}^{2}+\frac{2(1-\beta)\sigma^{2}}{b}T+\frac{4L^{2}\eta^{2}n}{(1-\beta)^{2}}T.

Finally, from the properties of variance and expectation,

𝔼⁡[‖Mt−∇f​(Wt)‖F]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\|M_{t}-\nabla f(W_{t})\|_{F}\right] ≤𝔼⁡[‖Mt−∇f​(Wt)‖F2]\displaystyle\leq\sqrt{\mathbb{E}\left[\|M_{t}-\nabla f(W_{t})\|_{F}^{2}\right]}
≤(1+β2)t​‖M0−∇f​(W0)‖F+2​(1−β)​σ2b+2​L​η​n(1−β).\displaystyle\leq\sqrt{\left(\frac{1+\beta}{2}\right)^{t}}\|M_{0}-\nabla f(W_{0})\|_{F}+\sqrt{\frac{2(1-\beta)\sigma^{2}}{b}}+\frac{2L\eta\sqrt{n}}{(1-\beta)}.

Hence, we have

∑t=0T−1𝔼⁡[‖Mt−∇f​(Wt)‖F]≤22−1+β​‖M0−∇f​(W0)‖F+2​(1−β)​σ2b​T+2​L​η​n1−β​T\displaystyle\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\mathbb{E}\left[\|M_{t}-\nabla f(W_{t})\|_{F}\right]\leq\frac{\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{2}-\sqrt{1+\beta}}\|M_{0}-\nabla f(W_{0})\|_{F}+\sqrt{\frac{2(1-\beta)\sigma^{2}}{b}}T+\frac{2L\eta\sqrt{n}}{1-\beta}T

This completes the proof. ∎

Appendix B Proof of Theorems for Muon without weight decay

Theorem B.1 (Auxiliary Theorem for Muon without weight decay).

Suppose that Assumptions 2.1-2.3 hold and the sequence (Wt)t∈ℕ(W_{t})_{t\in\mathbb{N}} generated by Muon without weight decay (Algorithm 1). Then for all t∈ℕt\in\mathbb{N},

∑t=0T−1𝔼⁡[‖∇f​(Wt)‖F]\displaystyle\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\mathbb{E}\left[\|\nabla f(W_{t})\|_{F}\right]
≤f⁡(W0)−f⁡(WT)η+12​∑t=0T−1𝔼⁡[‖∇f​(Wt)−Ct‖F2]+n​∑t=0T−1𝔼⁡[‖∇f​(Wt)−Ct‖F]+1+L​η2​n​T.\displaystyle\hskip 9.24994pt\leq\frac{f(W_{0})-f(W_{T})}{\eta}+\frac{1}{2}\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\mathbb{E}\left[\|\nabla f(W_{t})-C_{t}\|_{F}^{2}\right]+\sqrt{n}\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\mathbb{E}\left[\|\nabla f(W_{t})-C_{t}\|_{F}\right]+\frac{1+L\eta}{2}nT.
Proof.

From Assumption 2.1,

f⁡(Wt+1)\displaystyle f(W_{t+1}) ≤f⁡(Wt)+⟨∇f​(Wt),Wt+1−Wt⟩F+L2​‖Wt+1−Wt‖F2\displaystyle\leq f(W_{t})+\langle\nabla f(W_{t}),W_{t+1}-W_{t}\rangle_{F}+\frac{L}{2}\|W_{t+1}-W_{t}\|_{F}^{2}
=f⁡(Wt)−η​⟨∇f​(Wt),Ot⟩F+L2​η2​‖Ot‖F2\displaystyle=f(W_{t})-\eta\langle\nabla f(W_{t}),O_{t}\rangle_{F}+\frac{L}{2}\eta^{2}\|O_{t}\|_{F}^{2}
=f⁡(Wt)−η​⟨Ct,Ot⟩F−η​⟨∇f​(Wt)−Mt,Ot⟩F+L​η2​n2.\displaystyle=f(W_{t})-\eta\langle C_{t},O_{t}\rangle_{F}-\eta\langle\nabla f(W_{t})-M_{t},O_{t}\rangle_{F}+\frac{L\eta^{2}n}{2}.

Here, from Ot:=argminO:O⊤​O=In∥O−Ct∥FO_{t}:=\underset{O:O^{\top}O=I_{n}}{\operatorname{argmin}}\|O-C_{t}\|_{F}, we have Ot:=argmaxO:O⊤​O=In⟨Ct,O⟩FO_{t}:=\underset{O:O^{\top}O=I_{n}}{\operatorname{argmax}}\langle C_{t},O\rangle_{F}. Then,

⟨Ct,Ot⟩F=maxO:O⊤​O=In⟨Ct,O⟩F=maxO:‖O‖2≤1⟨Ct,O⟩F=:∥Ct∥∗,\displaystyle\langle C_{t},O_{t}\rangle_{F}=\max_{O:O^{\top}O=I_{n}}\langle C_{t},O\rangle_{F}=\max_{O:\|O\|_{2}\leq 1}\langle C_{t},O\rangle_{F}=:\|C_{t}\|_{*},

where ∥⋅∥∗\|\cdot\|_{*} denotes the dual norm. Hence, from reverse triangle inequality and ‖A‖F≤‖A‖∗≤rank​(A)​‖A‖F\|A\|_{F}\leq\|A\|_{*}\leq\sqrt{\text{rank}(A)}\|A\|_{F}, we have

−⟨Ct,Ot⟩F\displaystyle-\langle C_{t},O_{t}\rangle_{F} =−‖Ct‖∗\displaystyle=-\|C_{t}\|_{*}
=−‖Ct−∇f​(Wt)+∇f​(Wt)‖∗\displaystyle=-\|C_{t}-\nabla f(W_{t})+\nabla f(W_{t})\|_{*}
≤‖Ct−∇f​(Wt)‖∗−‖∇f​(Wt)‖∗\displaystyle\leq\|C_{t}-\nabla f(W_{t})\|_{*}-\|\nabla f(W_{t})\|_{*}
≤rank​(Ct−∇f​(Wt))​‖Ct−∇f​(Wt)‖F−‖∇f​(Wt)‖F\displaystyle\leq\sqrt{\text{rank}(C_{t}-\nabla f(W_{t}))}\|C_{t}-\nabla f(W_{t})\|_{F}-\|\nabla f(W_{t})\|_{F}
≤n​‖Ct−∇f​(Wt)‖F−‖∇f​(Wt)‖F.\displaystyle\leq\sqrt{n}\|C_{t}-\nabla f(W_{t})\|_{F}-\|\nabla f(W_{t})\|_{F}. (1)

In addition, we have

Appendix C Proof of Theorems for Muon with weight decay

C.1 Proof of Proposition 3.1

Proof.

From the definition of WtW_{t} and η≤1λ\eta\leq\frac{1}{\lambda}, we have

‖Wt‖F\displaystyle\|W_{t}\|_{F} =‖(1−η​λ)​Wt−1−η​Ot‖F\displaystyle=\|(1-\eta\lambda)W_{t-1}-\eta O_{t}\|_{F}

≤(1−η​λ)t​‖W0‖F+η​n​∑k=0t−1(1−η​λ)k\displaystyle\leq(1-\eta\lambda)^{t}\|W_{0}\|_{F}+\eta\sqrt{n}\sum_{k=0}^{t-1}(1-\eta\lambda)^{k}
≤(1−η​λ)t​‖W0‖F+nλ\displaystyle\leq(1-\eta\lambda)^{t}\|W_{0}\|_{F}+\frac{\sqrt{n}}{\lambda}
≤(1−η​λ)t​‖W0‖F+nλ.\displaystyle\leq(1-\eta\lambda)^{t}\|W_{0}\|_{F}+\frac{\sqrt{n}}{\lambda}.

C.2 Proof of Proposition 3.2

Proof.

According to Assumption 2.1,

‖∇f​(Wt)−∇f​(W⋆)‖F≤L​‖Wt−W⋆‖F.\displaystyle\|\nabla f(W_{t})-\nabla f(W^{\star})\|_{F}\leq L\|W_{t}-W^{\star}\|_{F}.

≤L​(1−η​λ)t​‖W0‖F+L​nλ+L​‖W⋆‖F.\displaystyle\leq L(1-\eta\lambda)^{t}\|W_{0}\|_{F}+\frac{L\sqrt{n}}{\lambda}+L\|W^{\star}\|_{F}.

Lemma C.1.

Suppose that Assumptions 2.1-2.3 hold and the sequence (Wt)t∈ℕ(W_{t})_{t\in\mathbb{N}} generated by Muon (Algorithm 1) with η≤1λ\eta\leq\frac{1}{\lambda}. Then, for all t∈ℕt\in\mathbb{N},

=𝔼⁡[‖∇f𝒮t​(Wt)‖F2]−‖∇f​(Wt)‖F2.\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\left[\|\nabla f_{\mathcal{S}_{t}}(W_{t})\|_{F}^{2}\right]-\|\nabla f(W_{t})\|_{F}^{2}.

Then, from Lemma A.1 and Proposition 3.2, we have

𝔼⁡[‖∇f𝒮t​(Wt)‖F2]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\|\nabla f_{\mathcal{S}_{t}}(W_{t})\|_{F}^{2}\right] ≤σ2b+‖∇f​(Wt)‖22\displaystyle\leq\frac{\sigma^{2}}{b}+\|\nabla f(W_{t})\|_{2}^{2}
≤σ2b+D02.\displaystyle\leq\frac{\sigma^{2}}{b}+D_{0}^{2}.

Hence, we have

∑t=0T−1𝔼⁡[‖∇f𝒮t​(Wt)‖F2]≤(σ2b+D02)​T.\displaystyle\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\mathbb{E}\left[\|\nabla f_{\mathcal{S}_{t}}(W_{t})\|_{F}^{2}\right]\leq\left(\frac{\sigma^{2}}{b}+D_{0}^{2}\right)T.

≤β​𝔼​[‖Mt−1‖F2]+(1−β)​𝔼​[‖∇f𝒮t​(Wt)‖F2]\displaystyle\leq\beta\mathbb{E}\left[\|M_{t-1}\|_{F}^{2}\right]+(1-\beta)\mathbb{E}\left[\|\nabla f_{\mathcal{S}_{t}}(W_{t})\|_{F}^{2}\right]
≤β​𝔼​[‖Mt−1‖F2]+(1−β)​(σ2b+Dt2)\displaystyle\leq\beta\mathbb{E}\left[\|M_{t-1}\|_{F}^{2}\right]+(1-\beta)\left(\frac{\sigma^{2}}{b}+D_{t}^{2}\right)
≤βt+1​‖M−1‖F2+(1−β)​(σ2b+D02)​∑k=0tβk\displaystyle\leq\beta^{t+1}\|M_{-1}\|_{F}^{2}+(1-\beta)\left(\frac{\sigma^{2}}{b}+D_{0}^{2}\right)\sum_{k=0}^{t}\beta^{k}

where we use M−1:=𝟎M_{-1}:=\bm{0}. Therefore, we have

∑t=0T−1𝔼⁡[‖Mt‖F2]≤(σ2b+D02)​T.\displaystyle\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\mathbb{E}\left[\|M_{t}\|_{F}^{2}\right]\leq\left(\frac{\sigma^{2}}{b}+D_{0}^{2}\right)T.

Theorem C.1 (Auxiliary Theorem for Muon with weight decay).

Suppose that Assumptions 2.1-2.3 hold and the sequence (Wt)t∈ℕ(W_{t})_{t\in\mathbb{N}} generated by Muon without weight decay (Algorithm 1). Then for all t∈ℕt\in\mathbb{N},

+λ2∑t=0T−1𝔼[∥Ct∥F2]+λ{1+2​(1+L​η)​λ2}∑t=0T−1𝔼[∥Wt∥F2]+(1+Lη)nT\displaystyle\hskip 9.24994pt+\frac{\lambda}{2}\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\mathbb{E}\left[\|C_{t}\|_{F}^{2}\right]+\lambda\left\{\frac{1+2(1+L\eta)\lambda}{2}\right\}\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\mathbb{E}\left[\|W_{t}\|_{F}^{2}\right]+(1+L\eta)nT
Proof.

f⁡(Wt+1)\displaystyle f(W_{t+1}) ≤f⁡(Wt)+⟨∇f​(Wt),Wt+1−Wt⟩F+L2​‖Wt+1−Wt‖F2\displaystyle\leq f(W_{t})+\langle\nabla f(W_{t}),W_{t+1}-W_{t}\rangle_{F}+\frac{L}{2}\|W_{t+1}-W_{t}\|_{F}^{2}
=f⁡(Wt)−η​⟨∇f​(Wt),Ot+λ​Wt⟩F+L​η22​‖Ot+λ​Wt‖F2\displaystyle=f(W_{t})-\eta\langle\nabla f(W_{t}),O_{t}+\lambda W_{t}\rangle_{F}+\frac{L\eta^{2}}{2}\|O_{t}+\lambda W_{t}\|_{F}^{2}
=f⁡(Wt)−η​⟨Ct,Ot+λ​Wt⟩F−η​⟨∇f​(Wt)−Ct,Ot+λ​Wt⟩F+L​η22​‖Ot+λ​Wt‖F2\displaystyle=f(W_{t})-\eta\langle C_{t},O_{t}+\lambda W_{t}\rangle_{F}-\eta\langle\nabla f(W_{t})-C_{t},O_{t}+\lambda W_{t}\rangle_{F}+\frac{L\eta^{2}}{2}\|O_{t}+\lambda W_{t}\|_{F}^{2}
=f⁡(Wt)−η​⟨Ct,Ot⟩F−η​λ​⟨Ct,Wt⟩F−η​⟨∇f​(Wt)−Ct,Ot+λ​Wt⟩F+L​η22​‖Ot+λ​Wt‖F2.\displaystyle=f(W_{t})-\eta\langle C_{t},O_{t}\rangle_{F}-\eta\lambda\langle C_{t},W_{t}\rangle_{F}-\eta\langle\nabla f(W_{t})-C_{t},O_{t}+\lambda W_{t}\rangle_{F}+\frac{L\eta^{2}}{2}\|O_{t}+\lambda W_{t}\|_{F}^{2}.

From Eq.(1), we have

−η​⟨Ct,Ot⟩F\displaystyle-\eta\langle C_{t},O_{t}\rangle_{F} ≤η​n​‖Ct−∇f​(Wt)‖F−η​‖∇f​(Wt)‖F.\displaystyle\leq\eta\sqrt{n}\|C_{t}-\nabla f(W_{t})\|_{F}-\eta\|\nabla f(W_{t})\|_{F}.

Hence, from ‖Ot+λ​Wt‖F2≤2​‖Ot‖F2+2​λ2​‖Wt‖F2\|O_{t}+\lambda W_{t}\|_{F}^{2}\leq 2\|O_{t}\|_{F}^{2}+2\lambda^{2}\|W_{t}\|_{F}^{2}, we have

Appendix D Analysis of critical batch size for Muon

Following earlier studies [19, 20], we derive Proposition 4.1 for estimating a lower bound on the critical batch size. First, the convergence of the optimizer must be analyzed (Theorems 3.1-3.4), and on the basis of that analysis, the number of steps TT required for training is defined as a function of batch size bb (Theorem D.1). Next, computational complexity is expressed as the number of steps multiplied by the batch size, and computational complexity T⁡(b)​bT(b)b is defined as a function of batch size bb. Finally, we identify critical batch size b⋆b^{\star} that minimizes computational complexity function T⁡(b)​bT(b)b (Theorem D.2) and transform the lower bound for each optimizer (Proposition 4.1).

D.1 Relationship between batch size and number of steps needed for training

Suppose that Assumptions 2.1-2.3 hold and sequence (Wt)t∈ℕ(W_{t})_{t\in\mathbb{N}} generated by Muon. Then, according to Theorems 3.1-3.4, the following hold:

1T​∑t=0T−1𝔼⁡[‖∇f​(Wt)‖F]≤XT+Yb+Z.\displaystyle\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\mathbb{E}\left[\|\nabla f(W_{t})\|_{F}\right]\leq\frac{X}{T}+\frac{Y}{b}+Z.

For example, for Muon without Nesterov and weight decay, from Theorem 3.1, the following hold:

1T​∑t=0T−1𝔼⁡[‖∇f​(Wt)‖F]\displaystyle\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\mathbb{E}\left[\|\nabla f(W_{t})\|_{F}\right] ≤(f⁡(W0)−f⁡(WT)η+‖M0−∇f​(W0)‖F2(1−β)+2​n​‖M0−∇f​(W0)‖F(2−1+β))⏟=:X1T\displaystyle\leq\underbrace{\left(\frac{f(W_{0})-f(W_{T})}{\eta}+\frac{\|M_{0}-\nabla f(W_{0})\|_{F}^{2}}{(1-\beta)}+\frac{\sqrt{2n}\|M_{0}-\nabla f(W_{0})\|_{F}}{(\sqrt{2}-\sqrt{1+\beta})}\right)}_{=:X}\frac{1}{T}
+(1−β)​σ2⏟=:Y1b+2​(1−β)​n​σ2+2​L2​η2​n(1−β)2+2​L​η​n1−β+1+L​η2​n⏟=:Z\displaystyle\hskip 9.24994pt+\underbrace{(1-\beta)\sigma^{2}}_{=:Y}\frac{1}{b}+\underbrace{\sqrt{2(1-\beta)n\sigma^{2}}+\frac{2L^{2}\eta^{2}n}{(1-\beta)^{2}}+\frac{2L\eta n}{1-\beta}+\frac{1+L\eta}{2}n}_{=:Z}
=XT+Yb+Z\displaystyle=\frac{X}{T}+\frac{Y}{b}+Z

When training is sufficiently complete, 1T​∑t=0T−1𝔼⁡[‖∇f​(Wt)‖F]<ϵ\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\mathbb{E}\left[\|\nabla f(W_{t})\|_{F}\right]<\epsilon holds for a sufficiently small threshold ϵ\epsilon. Here, YY and ZZ are constants independent of TT, so no matter how large the number of iterations TT is, they will not become small, and the norm of the gradient will converge to Yb+Z\frac{Y}{b}+Z as T→∞T\to\infty. Therefore, in order to understand the relationship between the batch size and the number of iterations required for training, we assume that the following holds when training is sufficiently complete:

XT+Yb<ϵ.\displaystyle\frac{X}{T}+\frac{Y}{b}<\epsilon. (4)

The relationship between bb and number of steps TMuon​(b)T_{\text{Muon}}(b) satisfying Eq. (4) is as follows:

Theorem D.1.

Suppose that Assumptions 2.1-2.3 hold and consider Muon. Then, TMuon​(b)T_{\text{Muon}}(b) defined by

TMuon​(b):=X​bϵ​b−Y<T​ for ​b>Yϵ,\displaystyle T_{\text{Muon}}(b):=\frac{Xb}{\epsilon b-Y}<T\text{\ \ for \ }b>\frac{Y}{\epsilon}, (5)

Muon satisfy Eq. (4). In addition, the functions TMuon​(b)T_{\text{Muon}}(b) defined by Eq. (5) is monotone decreasing and convex for b>Yϵb>\frac{Y}{\epsilon}.

Proof.

According to Eq. (5), Muon satisfy Eq. (4). We have that, for b>Yϵb>\frac{Y}{\epsilon},

d​TMuon​(b)d​b=−X​Y(ϵ​b−Y)2≤0,d2​TMuon​(b)d​b2=2​X​Y​ϵ(ϵ​b−Y)3≥0.\displaystyle\frac{\mathrm{d}T_{\text{Muon}}(b)}{\mathrm{d}b}=\frac{-XY}{(\epsilon b-Y)^{2}}\leq 0,\ \ \frac{\mathrm{d}^{2}T_{\text{Muon}}(b)}{\mathrm{d}b^{2}}=\frac{2XY\epsilon}{(\epsilon b-Y)^{3}}\geq 0.

Therefore, TMuon​(b)T_{\text{Muon}}(b) is monotone decreasing and convex for b>Yϵb>\frac{Y}{\epsilon}. This completes the proof. ∎

D.2 Existence of a critical batch size

The critical batch size minimizes the computational complexity for training. Here, we use SFO complexity as a measure of computational complexity. Since the stochastic gradient is computed bb times per step, SFO complexity is defined as

TMuon​(b)​b=X​b2ϵ​b−Y.\displaystyle T_{\text{Muon}}(b)b=\frac{Xb^{2}}{\epsilon b-Y}. (6)

The following theorem guarantees the existence of critical batch sizes that are global minimizers of TMuon​(b)​bT_{\text{Muon}}(b)b defined by Eq. (6).

Theorem D.2.

Suppose that Assumptions 2.1-2.3 hold and consider Muon. Then, there exists

bMuon⋆:=2​Yϵ\displaystyle b_{\text{Muon}}^{\star}:=\frac{2Y}{\epsilon} (7)

such that bMuon⋆b_{\text{Muon}}^{\star} minimizes the convex function TMuon​(b)​bT_{\text{Muon}}(b)b.

Proof.

From Equation (7), we have that, for b>Yϵb>\frac{Y}{\epsilon},

d​TMuon​(b)​bd​b=X​b​(ϵ​b−2​Y)(ϵ​b−Y)2,d2​TMuon​(b)​bd​b2=2​X​Y2(ϵ​b−Y)3≥0.\displaystyle\frac{\mathrm{d}T_{\text{Muon}}(b)b}{\mathrm{d}b}=\frac{Xb(\epsilon b-2Y)}{(\epsilon b-Y)^{2}},\ \ \frac{\mathrm{d}^{2}T_{\text{Muon}}(b)b}{\mathrm{d}b^{2}}=\frac{2XY^{2}}{(\epsilon b-Y)^{3}}\geq 0.

Hence, TMuon​(b)​bT_{\text{Muon}}(b)b is convex for b>Yϵb>\frac{Y}{\epsilon} and

d​TMuon​(b)​bd​b​{<0 if ​b<bMuon⋆,=0 if ​b=bMuon⋆=2​Yϵ,>0 if ​b>bMuon⋆.\displaystyle\frac{\mathrm{d}T_{\text{Muon}}(b)b}{\mathrm{d}b}\begin{cases}<0&\text{ if }b<b_{\text{Muon}}^{\star},\\ =0&\text{ if }b=b_{\text{Muon}}^{\star}=\frac{2Y}{\epsilon},\\ >0&\text{ if }b>b_{\text{Muon}}^{\star}.\end{cases}

This completes the proof. ∎

Appendix E Experimental Details

This section details the experimental setup for evaluating the optimizers. Our code will be available at https://github.com/Hiroki11x/critical_batchsize_muon.

Workloads and General Setup

All experiments are conducted on the CIFAR-10 dataset using a ResNet-18 model trained from scratch. Training is performed for a constant number of total samples seen, which is equivalent to 100 epochs at a batch size of 512. For any given batch size BB, the number of epochs is scaled as EB=100×(512/B)E_{B}=100\times(512/B). Each experiment was repeated 5 times with different random seeds, and we report the mean and standard deviation of the test accuracy.

Hyperparameter Tuning Protocol

We perform an extensive grid search over hyperparameters for each optimizer. The primary parameters tuned are the base learning rate (at a reference batch size of 512) and the weight decay coefficient. For batch sizes other than 512, we scale the learning rate from the base learning rate using the square root scaling rule, as specified in the main text:

ηB=η512×B512\eta_{B}=\eta_{512}\times\sqrt{\frac{B}{512}}

This scaling rule is applied to AdamW, Momentum SGD, and both components of Muon. For theoretical comparison, we also include results for Momentum SGD with a linear scaling rule (ηB∝B\eta_{B}\propto B).

The shared hyperparameter search space is detailed in Table 3. The optimizer-specific search spaces for learning rates and weight decay are presented in Table 4.

Optimizer Configuration

For the hybrid Muon optimizer, we apply the Muon update rule (Momentum SGD with a high momentum of 0.999) to all convolutional layers in the ResNet-18 model, excluding the initial input layer. All other parameters, including biases, batch normalization parameters, and the final linear layer, are updated using AdamW. The number of parameters handled by each optimizer component is listed in Table 5. For standard AdamW and Momentum SGD experiments, the respective optimizer is applied to all model parameters.

Appendix F Additional Results

This section provides supplementary results to support the analysis in the main text.

Convergence

Figure 5 shows the convergence rate comparison for ResNet-18 on CIFAR-10 with varying batch size. This complements Figure 2 by providing a clearer view of the effect of batch size.

Critical Batch Size

The analysis in Section 5.2 noted that Momentum SGD reaches a comparable accuracy to other optimizers, despite requiring more steps. Figure 4 demonstrate this, showing that while its convergence is slower, it does not stall at a lower accuracy.
